author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell revisits the biblical story of Joseph being betrayed by his brothers, stripped of his robe and thrown into an empty cistern. But rather than treating the well simply as a place of imprisonment, he explores it as something much deeper — a symbolic death, or even a kind of crucifixion, where Joseph’s old identity dies and the person who eventually emerges is fundamentally changed.

The story then moves to Judah’s intervention and the arrival of the Midianite merchants, who pull Joseph from the cistern before he is sold for twenty shekels of silver and taken toward Egypt.

From there, Russell widens the interpretation into something even more profound: the idea that biblical stories can point beyond ordinary history and into a reality outside space and time. And if we move beyond space and time, what remains? Eternity.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell reflects on a deceptively simple idea: maybe we don’t need to be entertained every second of the day. Learning to tolerate boredom, he suggests, can be part of reclaiming control over both the mind and the body. He connects this to Paul’s call not to conform to the patterns of the world, but to be transformed through the renewing of the mind — continually returning to the present instead of automatically obeying every impulse.

From compulsively checking your phone to reaching for another Oreo when you aren’t even hungry, the conversation explores how deeply physical cravings can shape our behavior. Russell’s guest argues that addiction isn’t simply something happening in your thoughts — the body itself begins demanding the pattern.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell reflects on Monty Python’s Life of Brian and one of its funniest scenes, where Brian tries to repeat fragments of what he remembers hearing from Jesus at the Sermon on the Mount — including the message not to worry and to “look at the birds.”

But beneath the comedy, Russell sees something deeper. He argues that when scripture is approached only through mockery, skepticism, or comedic scrutiny, it’s easy to miss the central message entirely: that you are made in the image of God.

The conversation ends on an even more challenging idea — that the painful and difficult things we experience may not simply be meaningless suffering, but part of the process through which we are being shaped and formed.
